target: हम आज बहुत थके हुए हैं, कल बात करते हैं।
english: We are very tired today, let us talk tomorrow.
tip: The plain present doubles as 'let's': कल बात करते हैं (kal baat karte hain = we talk tomorrow) actually offers 'let's talk tomorrow'. No extra word needed.

target: मेरी छोटी बेटी को रंगीन चित्र बनाना बहुत पसंद है।
english: My little daughter loves to draw colorful pictures.
tip: With पसंद है (pasand hai = is pleasing), the liker takes को (ko): बेटी को पसंद है (beti ko pasand hai) is literally 'to the daughter it is pleasing', not 'daughter likes'.

target: वह पूरी कक्षा में सबसे तेज़ और होशियार छात्र है।
english: He is the sharpest and smartest student in the whole class.
tip: Superlatives are 'from all': सबसे तेज़ (sabse tez = fast beyond all) = fastest. No -est ending in Hindi – सबसे (sabse) before any adjective does it.

target: मुझे यक़ीन है कि तुम यह काम ज़रूर कर सकते हो।
english: I am sure that you can definitely do this work.
tip: English can drop 'that' – 'I'm sure you can'. Hindi never drops कि: मुझे यक़ीन है कि (mujhe yaqeen hai ki = I'm sure that). The कि (ki) always stays.

target: यह वाला कितने का है?
english: How much is this one?
tip: वाला (wala) picks out a specific one: यह वाला (yeh wala) = this one. It works with colors, sizes, and prices in any shop.

target: मेरी चार बजे एक ज़रूरी मीटिंग है।
english: I have an important meeting at four.
tip: चार बजे (char baje = at four) is literally 'four struck' – Hindi counts clock time in bell strikes, so there is no separate word for 'o'clock'.

target: ज़रा मेरा फ़ोन ठीक कर दो।
english: Please fix my phone.
tip: दो (do = give) added to a verb aims the action at someone else: ठीक कर दो (theek kar do) = fix it for me. The 'give' points the favor toward the asker.

target: दुभाषिया ने दोनों भाषाओं में बात समझाई।
english: The interpreter explained the matter in both languages.
tip: ने (ne) only for action-on-something verbs in the past. मैं गया (main gaya = I went, no ne) vs मैंने देखा (mainne dekha = I saw, ne). Going has no "object".

target: आज मुझे बहुत सारा काम करना है।
english: I have a lot of work to do today.
tip: करना (karna = to do) is a core verb. काम करना (kaam karna = to work) pairs a noun with करना to make a verb.

target: मेरे पास अभी बात करने का समय नहीं है।
english: I don't have time to talk right now.
tip: Hindi has no verb 'to have' – things sit near you: मेरे पास (mere paas = near me) + समय नहीं है (samay nahin hai = there's no time) = I don't have time.

target: आपसे मिलकर खुशी हुई।
english: Nice to meet you.
tip: आपसे मिलकर खुशी हुई (aapse milkar khushi hui) is literally 'having met you, happiness happened' – joy is an event that occurs, not something you are.

target: यह कितने का है?
english: How much does this cost?
tip: Prices use 'of': यह कितने का है? (yah kitne ka hai) = 'this is of how much?'. The answer keeps का too – सौ का है (sau ka hai) = it's a hundred.

target: कैसे हो यार? सब ठीक-ठाक?
english: How are you, friend? All good?
tip: ठीक-ठाक (theek-thaak) doubles ठीक with a rhyming echo to soften it – 'more or less fine'. Hindi loves these pairs: चाय-वाय (chai-vai) = tea and such.

target: पिताजी हमारे परिवार के मुखिया हैं।
english: Father is the head of our family.
tip: Respect makes one person plural: पिताजी ... हैं (pitaji ... hain), not है – father gets the 'they' verb even though he is one man.

target: दोस्त, तुम्हारी बहुत याद आ रही थी।
english: Friend, I was missing you a lot.
tip: You don't miss someone – their memory comes to you: तुम्हारी याद आ रही थी (tumhari yaad aa rahi thi) = 'your memory was coming'.

target: मेरी बड़ी बहन की शादी पिछले साल हुई थी।
english: My elder sister got married last year.
tip: Weddings happen rather than being gotten: शादी हुई थी (shaadi hui thi) = 'the wedding happened'. Hindi treats marrying as an event, with होना (hona = happen).

target: कल मुझे एक नई मिठाई की दुकान मिली।
english: I found a new sweet shop yesterday.
tip: मिली (mili) is 'met' doing duty for 'found': the shop met you – दुकान मिली (dukaan mili). Things you find, get, or receive all 'meet' you in Hindi.

target: मेज़ पर किताबें रखी हैं।
english: Books are kept on the table.
tip: Hindi says how things got there: किताबें रखी हैं (kitaaben rakhi hain) = 'the books are kept'. Where English uses plain 'are', Hindi adds the placing verb.

target: रेलवे स्टेशन कितनी दूर है?
english: How far is the railway station?
tip: Question words don't jump to the front: कितनी दूर (kitni door = how far) sits right where the answer would – स्टेशन कितनी दूर है, no flipping around.

target: नदी के उस पार गाँव है।
english: There is a village on the other side of the river.
tip: Hindi's 'across' follows its noun: नदी के उस पार (nadi ke us paar) = 'the river's far side'. Position words come after the noun, not before it.

target: मेरे दादाजी पचहत्तर साल के हैं।
english: My grandfather is seventy-five years old.
tip: Age is something you are 'of': पचहत्तर साल के हैं (pachhattar saal ke hain) = 'is of seventy-five years'. No word for 'old' anywhere – के carries it.

target: मेरा भाई इंजीनियर बनना चाहता है।
english: My brother wants to become an engineer.
tip: No 'a' or 'an' in Hindi: इंजीनियर बनना (engineer banna) = 'to become engineer'. Articles don't exist – context does that work.

target: मेरी बिल्ली सोफ़े पर बैठी है।
english: My cat is sitting on the sofa.
tip: बैठी है (baithi hai) = 'is seated', a settled state. बैठ रही है would mean she is in the middle of sitting down. English '-ing' misleads here.

target: राहुल गाड़ी में बैठकर हैदराबाद गया।
english: Rahul went to Hyderabad by car.
tip: 'By car' is 'having sat in the car': गाड़ी में बैठकर (gaadi mein baithkar). The -कर (-kar) ending chains actions – sit, then go, in one sentence.

target: मज़बूत दरवाज़ा तूफ़ान में भी टिका रहा।
english: The strong door remained standing even in the storm.
tip: भी (bhi = even, also) follows the word it highlights: तूफ़ान में भी (toofan mein bhi) = 'even in the storm'. English puts 'even' first; Hindi tags it after.

target: मेरे बड़े भाई का कमरा ऊपर है।
english: My elder brother's room is upstairs.
tip: का matches the thing owned, not the owner: भाई का कमरा (bhai ka kamra) – का is masculine because कमरा is. Own a गाड़ी instead and it flips to की.

target: दूध ख़त्म हो गया, बाज़ार से ले आना।
english: The milk is finished, bring some from the market.
tip: 'Bring' is built from 'take' plus 'come': बाज़ार से ले आना (bazaar se le aana) = take from the market and come. ले जाना (le jaana = take plus go) is 'take away' – the second verb sets the direction.

target: सिरदर्द की गोली खाने से राहत मिली।
english: Taking the headache pill gave relief.
tip: Pills are eaten in Hindi: गोली खाने से (goli khaane se) = 'from eating the pill'. खाना stretches past food – even betrayal gets eaten: धोखा खाना (dhokha khaana) = to be betrayed.

target: बच्चे की किताब ज़मीन पर गिर गई।
english: The child's book fell on the ground.
tip: गिर गई (gir gayi) adds जाना (jaana = go) to the fall – it marks the action as complete and final. Tacking जाना onto a verb means fully done.

target: मुझे कल डॉक्टर से मिलना है।
english: I have to see the doctor tomorrow.
tip: 'Have to' is built with 'to me': मुझे ... मिलना है (mujhe milna hai) = 'to me is to-meet'. Obligation sits on you as मुझे + verb + है.
